name: Freya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills your workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the violins in a ballet orchestra, make rehearsal recordings and teach three advanced pupils. I have a music master’s and am usually the one who can pull a tired section back together after an awkward cue. I love the quiet count before the curtain; I dislike arguing over whether a dress rehearsal was paid.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that fit home now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner works at the water office, and our children are grown. We have a mortgage and four months of expenses saved, my season pays about the usual senior rate, and a few similar groups hire nearby. I keep paper parts and have never used AI for work; I prefer a signed call sheet and my ears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the players that quicker booking is fine if rehearsal and doubling fees for playing a second instrument remain on the signed sheet. I would still listen to the section before calling a passage ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ballet season, three pupils and my partner’s wage cover our mortgage. Four months saved gets us through an ordinary gap between productions, so this plateau feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep paid ballet and pupil hours and ask for written dress-rehearsal, doubling and cancellation rates. In the plateau’s first year I would request my actual pension estimate and compare it with mortgage and health before naming a retirement date, then save one tenth of any cleared extra recital fee after bills toward five months of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about booked work in this picture. A signed dress-rehearsal fee lets me put the violin away and sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is doubling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes play a second instrument in one show, which adds preparation and should add a fee. I want the extra amount written beside the call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you set a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I need an actual pension statement and our mortgage figures first. A birthday alone is not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the ballet office which recorded rehearsal cues and preparation hours remain paid when software books and makes parts. I would say a violin section still needs a leader who hears the dancers breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rehearsal recordings bring about a fifth of my own income, and I expect some buyers to switch to generated cues. Four months saved gives me time to negotiate, but that recurring fee would not replace itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid performances and pupils and ask the office for written recording-use and preparation rates. In disruption’s first year, if two monthly recording calls disappear, I would bring the invoices to the musicians association and ask for a written live section-leading and cancellation schedule; I would check actual cleared fees against mortgage dates rather than count an unsigned agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own recording pay shrinking. A strong section can still play, but it cannot invoice a buyer who has gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI arranging tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI and would first want an agreed paid use and a safe place for the score. For now I will read the printed part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the association guarantee a rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would bring the invoices and ask for terms; the employer still has to agree and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the strings that thinking AGI by 2028 could make rehearsal cues before robot violinists arrive around 2031. I would request signed live dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect recorded cues and some paid preparation to end in 2028, near a third of my own pay. I have woken up counting the mortgage instalments. The live ballet chair may hold until robots are closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would total cue and preparation invoices and keep signed ballet and pupil dates. In the first year after 2028, if those fees go, I would seek a posted paid conservatory ensemble-tutor role only if my music master’s and violin-section leadership meet its requirements, actual paid in-person coaching and preparation remain, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees with a workable train; I would keep current ballet and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about a large expected loss to my own income. Four months saved is time to compare a real tutor posting, not a promise that one will appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a tutor do in person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hear a player tense a bow arm and change the exercise beside the stand. A conservatory would have to post and pay for that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why search before robot players?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recording buyer can leave in 2028. Robot violinists are about three years later in this picture, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the ballet company that five years until thinking AGI by 2031 gives us time to write live rehearsal and preparation fees into the next contract. Robot violinists arrive around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some recordings to thin over those years, but the orchestra may still need an experienced leader in the room. A long contract would help only if it pays actual preparation and cancellations, not a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would ask the company for a written two-season agreement paying live section leadership, preparation and cancelled calls, and keep three pupils. In the first year after 2031 I would renew only if those paid terms cover my hours; if recorded cues and paid live rehearsals both fall, I would seek a posted paid ensemble-tutor role accepting my master’s and violin leadership, paid in-person coaching/preparation, and written net pay after travel replacing both lost fees with a workable train, keeping ballet and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the possible recording slide, with time to read a real contract. Five years can buy negotiation time, but not an unsigned rehearsal fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the ballet company offers a title without pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the preparation and cancellation rates on paper. I already lead the violins; a new title is not a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No course has shown me a paid place I need. I would first protect the work I already do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot violinists around 2039 are separate dates. I would still ask the ballet office to put the next live fee in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might choose fewer late shows, but I have not seen an actual pension estimate. Four months saved and our current wages cover the next few years; a decade may change recorded work without telling me when to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid ballet and pupils, request my actual pension estimate and written live renewal, then save one tenth of cleared extra recital fees after mortgage, food and travel toward five months of expenses. In the first year after 2036, if recording and live preparation fees fall, I would seek only a posted paid ensemble-tutor role accepting my master’s and violin-section leadership, paying in-person coaching/preparation, and offering written net pay after travel that replaces the loss with a workable train; I would keep current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant recording work while present live pay holds. I would look at a real pension statement before cutting a single paid rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire simply at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would compare an actual pension estimate, the mortgage and our health. We have no date set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no tutor role appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the booked paid ballet and pupil calls while they last. A degree cannot create an opening.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cues and preparation could take a third of my pay quickly. Signed ballet dates and a real tutor post paying live coaching with written net wages after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the section leader to mark every new violin bowing before the curtain. The audience hears a clean entrance, not the unpaid hour behind it.

headlineQuote: The audience hears a clean entrance, not the unpaid hour behind it.
portrait: Freya is a **senior violin leader** with a music master’s, ballet work, recordings and three advanced pupils.
She has **four months saved**, typical senior pay, a water-office partner, grown children and a mortgage.
She **never uses AI** and seeks written live terms before considering a posted paid tutor role.
She requests an **actual pension estimate** without assuming a retirement entitlement.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** could end cue and preparation fees worth near a third of her income.
